adds.title: Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria 1999-2006: A Sourcebook, Vol. IV, Ch. 4 Part IV — The Niger State Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (Ostien, ed.)
adds.summary: Ostien's sourcebook reproduces Niger State's own Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 in full — a law to amend Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State, to review the punishments therein, gazetted in the Niger State of Nigeria Gazette No. 8, Vol. 25 of 9 March 2000 (pp. B29-B36) and coming into force on 4 May 2000. The enactment defines 'adultery' to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment (with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68), while the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies. State-level statutory proof that Niger, like the other northern bloc states, built a distinct criminal track for Muslim defendants — the legal layer this record identifies as the visitor-facing risk beyond federal law.

adds.title: Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria 1999-2006: A Sourcebook, Vol. IV, Ch. 4 Part III — The Sharia Penal Codes (Ostien, ed.)
adds.summary: The annotated sourcebook catalogue records Niger: Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000, HB.4/2000, signed into law on 22 February 2000 and coming into operation on 4 May 2000 (Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8, 9 March 2000). The editor notes it is not a complete Sharia Penal Code: it merely amends the Penal Code of 1960 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims, and it is printed in its entirety in Part IV of the same chapter. Confirms the state-specific enactment behind this record's claim that an outed Muslim visitor in Niger State stands under a harsher parallel legal frame than federal law alone.

adds.title: Suspected Gay Escapes Being Killed By Mob In Benin City – The Nigerian Observer
adds.summary: On 10 June 2010 The Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City (Oredo LGA, Edo State) that a middle-aged man, Mark Osato Edomwonyi, narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was caught in a same-sex act with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment; a neighbour raised the alarm and Mark fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, which then 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution is recorded in the report, and Mark's whereabouts were still unknown at filing. First incident-level evidence for Edo beyond the 2018 Ekpoma killing: lethal mob 'community justice' operates in the state capital too, with no documented law-enforcement response.

adds.title: Police Declare Ugbogbo Ovbukhan Wanted Over Gay Practice – The Nigerian Observer
adds.summary: The Nigerian Observer reported on 15 August 2008 that police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were caught in the act in a remote community in Edo State in February 2008; a mob mercilessly beat the two for desecrating the community, Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived, and the police arrested Jerry for interrogation. Direct evidence that Edo's police machinery pursued same-sex couples on the ground in 2008 — a community lynching attempt answered by arrest and a wanted declaration rather than protection.

adds.title: 2023 Indonesian Penal Code – Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's article on the 2023 Indonesian Penal Code (RUU KUHP) records that the law was passed on 6 December 2022 and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after enactment, and that it criminalises sexual activity outside marriage — unmarried partners face up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The article notes the code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, and that because same-sex marriage is not recognised in Indonesia, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction. This is the national criminal baseline a visitor in Central Kalimantan stands under, consistent with this record's finding that the province's risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence.

adds.title: LGBT rights in Australia – Wikipedia
adds.summary: The article dates Tasmania's equality timeline precisely: after the Commonwealth Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994, Tasmania still refused to repeal its anti-gay Criminal Code provisions and, faced with a likely High Court loss in Croome v Tasmania, decriminalised male homosexuality with effect from 14 May 1997 — the final Australian jurisdiction to do so. It records that the age of consent in Tasmania is 17 (one of only two jurisdictions with South Australia), that same-sex couples can enter into domestic registered partnerships in Tasmania with an optional official ceremony, that equality of adoption rights for same-sex couples applied in all states and territories from April 2018, and that as of 2019 Tasmania issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates. Corroborates this record's account that Tasmania reached formal legal equality via the national framework with no state-specific incident series or enforcement pattern documented, while flagging the one standing statutory particularity — the 17 age of consent — not covered by the record's summary.

adds.title: Tasmania makes gender optional on birth certificates after Liberal crosses floor – ABC News
adds.summary: ABC News reported on 11 April 2019 that Tasmania's House of Assembly passed the Marriage Amendments Bill the previous day (10 April 2019) after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition, the legislation having already passed the Legislative Council. The reforms make gender on birth certificates optional, remove the requirement that transgender people undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised, and let people aged 16 or older change their registered gender without parental approval, with the Tasmanian Government having opposed the amendments and declining to rule out later repeal. State-specific enactment-level evidence for the equal-status finding in this record: the operational reform a trans visitor to Tasmania stands under, passed against government resistance rather than reflecting any criminalisation or incident series.

adds.title: LGBT rights in Australia – Wikipedia
adds.summary: The article's territory notes are directly on point for the external territories: Norfolk Island has been incorporated into NSW legislation from 1 July 2016 under the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015 and the Territories Legislation Amendment Act 2016, and Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands — the Australian Indian Ocean Territories — are jurisdictions where WA laws apply. The page also records that 'X' sex-descriptor availability and anti-discrimination protection on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression extend across the states and territories with concurrent federal protection, and that same-sex adult private sexual conduct has been legal nationally since the Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994. As the national-framework document for dependent territories governed directly by Commonwealth law, it supports this record's finding that visitors to Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and Jervis Bay territory stand under the national/NSW/WA framework with no territory-specific SOGIE provision or divergence documented.

adds.title: Sex Discrimination Act 1984 – Wikipedia
adds.summary: The article records that the Commonwealth Sex Discrimination Act 1984 was amended by the Sex Discrimination Amendment (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Intersex Status) Act 2013, so that discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status is prohibited — alongside sex, marital or relationship status, pregnancy and breastfeeding — across areas of public life including work, accommodation, education and the provision of goods and services. As a Commonwealth statute applying throughout Australia, including the external territories governed directly by Commonwealth law, this is the anti-discrimination framework a visitor on Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands or Jervis Bay territory stands under, confirming the national layer this record identifies with no locally diverging provision on the record.
